# Typewriter (`typewriter`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/communication.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Communication & information (`communication`)
- Deps: helped by interchangeable_parts, precision_measurement, alphabet_writing
- Core idea: Each key works a lever that swings a type slug against an inked ribbon onto paper held on a rubber roller (platen); an escapement moves the carriage one letter width after each stroke, a lever turns the roller one line, and a shift moves the type so each slug carries two characters. It writes uniform, legible text faster than a pen and makes several copies at once with carbon paper. It needs many small precise steel parts and springs, so it became practical only with mass production.
- Pitfalls:
  - Building it before cheap precision parts exist: dozens of earlier designs were single, hand-made curiosities
  - Repeating that QWERTY was designed to slow typists: the layout evolved over several designs; the precise role of type-bar jams is disputed
  - Assuming it cannot work for Chinese: Chinese typewriters with trays of some 2,500 characters were made from the 1910s
- History: europe: 1714 – Henry Mill's English patent (no machine known); 1808 Pellegrino Turri builds a machine for a blind countess; 1865–1870 Malling-Hansen's writing ball in Denmark, sold commercially; americas: 1868 – Sholes, Glidden and Soule patent; 1874 Remington No. 1; 1878 shift key (Remington No. 2); east_asia: 1915 – Sugimoto Kyōta's Japanese typewriter; china: 1916 – Zhou Houkun's Chinese typewriter; 1920s Commercial Press models
- Read:
  - Richard N. Current, The Typewriter and the Men Who Made It (1954)
  - Thomas S. Mullaney, The Chinese Typewriter: A History (2017)
